## 1. ZINC (Zn)

### 1.1 General Background and Essentiality

Zinc is an essential trace element that plays a fundamental physiological role in numerous cellular processes. Approximately 10% of the proteins in the human body exert their functions by binding with zinc and controlling various physiological responses at the molecular level [Zinc in Cardiovascular Functions and Diseases: IJMS, 2023]. Zinc is an essential micronutrient involved in over 300 enzymes and 2,000 transcriptional factors, with critical roles in cell differentiation, DNA synthesis, immune function, and antioxidant defense [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021]. The human body contains 2–3 g of zinc, with approximately 57% and 29% of total body zinc existing in skeletal muscle and bone, respectively; heart and blood plasma are known to contain 0.4% and 0.1% of body zinc [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].

Zinc deficiency affects 17% of the global population, up to 35% in low-income populations (i.e., South Asia and Africa) [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021]. Zinc deficiency may affect up to two billion people worldwide [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018]. The recommended daily zinc intake is 11 mg/day for men and 8 mg/day for women, with a maximum of 40 mg/day [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025].

### 1.2 Zinc's Role in Oxidative Stress

Zinc is not redox-active itself but protects against oxidative stress through multiple indirect mechanisms, including: competing with redox-active metals (e.g., iron, copper) for binding sites, stabilizing sulfhydryl groups, accelerating metallothionein (MT) synthesis, and serving as a cofactor in antioxidant enzymes like SOD1 (copper-zinc superoxide dismutase) [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].

Zinc deficiency leads to increased oxidative stress through NMDA receptor activation, NADPH oxidase stimulation, and reduced antioxidant enzyme activity [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025]. Zinc deficiency increases oxidative stress, NF-κB DNA binding activity, COX-2 and E-selectin gene expression, and monocyte adhesion in cultured porcine aortic endothelial cells [Zinc Deficiency and Mechanisms of Endothelial Cell Dysfunction: UKY Dissertation, 2008].

### 1.3 Zinc's Role in Inflammation

Zinc deficiency leads to increased activation of NF-κB and inflammatory cytokine expression (including IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ), while zinc supplementation suppresses NF-κB activation [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018]. Zinc deficiency down-regulates PPARα expression and PPAR DNA binding activity in endothelial cells, and compromises PPARγ transactivation activity [Zinc Deficiency and Mechanisms of Endothelial Cell Dysfunction: UKY Dissertation, 2008]. The anti-inflammatory properties of rosiglitazone (a PPARγ agonist) were compromised during zinc deficiency [Zinc Deficiency and Mechanisms of Endothelial Cell Dysfunction: UKY Dissertation, 2008].

### 1.4 Zinc's Role in Endothelial Function

Zinc deficiency contributes to endothelial dysfunction through disruption of eNOS and Nrf2/HO-1 signaling, leading to impaired nitric oxide bioavailability [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025]. Zinc deficiency contributes to endothelial damage, atherosclerosis, hypertension, heart failure, left ventricular hypertrophy, ischemic stroke, and coronary artery disease through mechanisms including increased oxidative stress, inflammation (IL-6, TNF-α), disrupted nitric oxide signaling, and impaired fatty acid/carbohydrate metabolism [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021].

### 1.5 Zinc Transporters and Cardiovascular Function

Intracellular zinc homeostasis is regulated by ZIP transporters (zinc influx into cytoplasm) and ZnT transporters (zinc efflux from cytoplasm or into organelles), along with metallothioneins. Twenty-four zinc transporters are found within the human heart muscle tissue, so disturbances in zinc homeostasis may lead to CVDs [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021].

Specific zinc transporters relevant to cardiovascular function include: ZnT1 (modulates L-type calcium channels), ZnT5 (KO mice show brady-arrhythmias and sudden death), ZIP2 (cardioprotective against ischemia/reperfusion injury), ZIP8 (cardiac ventricular compaction), and ZIP13 (cardiac remodeling, arrhythmia, and aortic fragility; downregulated by stress) [Zinc in Cardiovascular Functions and Diseases: IJMS, 2023].

Transporters abundant in heart tissues include ZIP1, ZIP7, ZIP13, ZIP14, ZnT9; in endothelial cells: ZIP1, ZIP13, ZnT5; in smooth muscle cells: ZIP6, ZIP1, ZIP13, ZnT1, ZnT5, ZnT9 [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].

Zinc acts as a signaling molecule ("zinc signals") through zinc transporters (SLC39A/ZIP and SLC30A/ZnT families) and other membrane proteins, regulating cellular processes including oxidative stress, inflammation, and calcium homeostasis. Other membrane proteins regulating zinc homeostasis in cardiovascular tissues include GPR39, TRPA1, TRPC6, RyR2, and MG23 [Zinc in Cardiovascular Functions and Diseases: IJMS, 2023].

### 1.6 Zinc Deficiency and Cardiovascular Disease

Zinc deficiency accelerates atherosclerosis through multiple mechanisms: increased oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, altered lipid metabolism (impaired fatty acid synthesis, changes in HDL/LDL, increased triglycerides), impaired immune function (reduced thymulin, T-cell imbalance, chronic inflammation), and affected platelet function [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025].

Epidemiological studies suggest that low plasma/serum zinc levels increase the risk of developing cardiovascular diseases, while supplementation of zinc may decrease this risk [Zinc in Cardiovascular Functions and Diseases: IJMS, 2023]. Lower serum zinc levels are associated with higher CVD risk, particularly in vulnerable populations (diabetes patients, those undergoing coronary angiography) [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021].

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey found that zinc intake at recommended levels (OR = 0.82; 95% CI: 0.69–0.98) was associated with a 0.82-fold greater than 20% risk of ASCVD over 10 years, regardless of the patient's gender, age, or lipid-lowering therapy [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025].

A study from the University of St Andrews (2025) found that low zinc was associated with a higher risk of developing MACE, and low zinc was associated with increased risks of various circulatory diseases [Abnormal plasma/serum magnesium, copper and zinc concentrations: Nutrients, 2025].

### 1.7 Zinc Excess and Cardiovascular Disease

Zinc overload can also induce oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and copper deficiency, all contributing to atherogenesis [Role of zinc in atherosclerosis: J Xiangya Medicine, 2025].

### 1.8 Zinc Supplementation

Zinc interventions have atheroprotective effects, improve lipid profiles (increase HDL-C, lower TC, LDL-C, TG), support myocardial healing, reduce arrhythmias, and improve glycemic control [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021]. Long-duration and low-dose supplementation was found to be more beneficial than short-duration (less than 12 weeks) and high-dose (more than 25 mg/day) zinc supplementation [Zinc in Cardiovascular Functions and Diseases: IJMS, 2023]. Low-dose and long-duration zinc interventions are of identical or in some instances of even larger magnitude and with even more beneficial effects compared to high-dose and short-duration interventions [Zinc as a Biomarker of Cardiovascular Health: Frontiers in Nutrition, 2021].

Serum zinc may work together with other cardiac markers as prognostic markers for MI. Serum zinc levels fall significantly after MI, with prognostic implications. Zinc supplementation in animal studies reduced infarct size. There is an inverse association between plasma zinc concentrations and postoperative atrial fibrillation [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].

### 1.9 Zinc in Cardiac Fibrosis

Zinc ion homeostasis affects metallothionein (MT) expression levels, which in turn influences cardiac fibrosis [Redox homeostasis in cardiac fibrosis: Redox Biology, 2024].

### 1.10 Zinc Status in Specific CVDs

- **Hypertension**: Altered zinc distribution between extracellular and intracellular spaces is observed [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].
- **Myocardial Infarction**: Serum zinc levels fall significantly after MI, with prognostic implications [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].
- **Atrial Fibrillation**: Inverse association between plasma zinc concentrations and postoperative AF [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].
- **Congestive Heart Failure**: Association between zinc deficiency and heart failure, with hypozincemia observed in patients [Zinc deficiency and cellular oxidative stress: Acta Pharmacologica Sinica, 2018].

## 2. COPPER (Cu)

### 2.1 General Background

Copper is an essential trace element obtained from diet (vegetables, shellfish, meat, seeds, nuts). It exists in two ionic forms: Cu⁺ (cuprous) and Cu²⁺ (copper ion). Copper metabolism involves three stages: absorption (via CTR1), transportation (via chaperone proteins including COX17, CCS, ATOX1, ATP7A, ATP7B), and excretion. Copper is crucial for energy metabolism, mitochondrial respiration, and antioxidant activity [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024]. The WHO recommends 0.9 mg/day copper intake for adults (70 kg) [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.2 Copper's Role in Lipid Metabolism

Dysregulation of copper ions can disturb lipid metabolism, resulting in oxidative stress, mitochondrial damage and endothelial cell dysfunction, and induce atherosclerosis and other cardiovascular diseases such as arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.3 Copper's Role in Oxidative Stress via Fenton Chemistry

Excess copper cycles through oxidation/reduction generating hydroxyl radicals, causing DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, and GSH oxidation. Copper-mediated Fenton reactions disrupt the TCA cycle, inducing proteotoxic stress and cell death [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.4 Copper/Zinc Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1)

The copper-zinc superoxide dismutase system (SOD1) catalyzes the conversion of the potentially toxic superoxide anion (O₂·⁻) to the less toxic substance hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and dioxygen (O₂). The catalytic mechanism involves two redox steps: Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu¹⁺ as superoxide is oxidized to O₂, then Cu¹⁺ is re-oxidized to Cu²⁺ as a second superoxide molecule is reduced to H₂O₂. The copper ion acts as an electron transfer center, while the zinc ion serves as a structural scaffold and contributes to the positive charge of the active site, which attracts the negatively charged superoxide anion [Cu/Zn Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1): Chemistry LibreTexts].

SOD1 is ubiquitous in mammalian cells and is expressed at relatively high levels in blood vessels; in normal mouse aorta the activity of SOD1 accounts for a significant portion of antioxidant defense [The Cu, Zn Superoxide Dismutase: Not Only a Dismutase Enzyme: PMC, 2016]. Three types of mammalian SOD exist: SOD1 (cytoplasmic Cu/Zn), SOD2 (mitochondrial matrix Mn), and SOD3 (extracellular Cu/Zn) [Cu/Zn Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1): Chemistry LibreTexts].

SOD1 knockout causes hypercholesterolemia and hypotriglyceridemia with irregular lipid accumulation in liver, heart, kidney, muscle and testis. The significant increase of sterol regulatory element binding proteins (SREBP) 2 and decrease of SREBP1 in SOD1⁻/⁻ mice were observed. Knockout of SOD1 caused disorder in lipid metabolism associated with the increased transcription of genes involved in cholesterol synthesis [Impact of SOD1 Knockout on Lipid Metabolism in Mice: Cornell eCommons, 2009].

SOD1 overexpression reduced cardiac allograft damage and the production of chemokines and adhesion molecules in the cardiac allograft [Overexpression of Human Cu/Zn SOD: AHA Journals].

### 2.5 Copper and Mitochondrial Dysfunction

Copper deficiency reduces CCO activity and mitochondrial function, leading to cardiomyocyte stiffening and fatal CVD. Copper excess alters energy metabolism by binding to thioctylated proteins in the TCA cycle [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.6 Copper and Vascular Regulation

Copper influences HIF-1-mediated angiogenesis, LOX production, and vascular wall tone. Both copper excess and deficiency impair vascular function [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.7 Copper Excess and Cardiovascular Disease

Excess copper is linked to arrhythmia, atherosclerosis, heart failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic aneurysms, and myocardial injury. Multiple human studies show positive correlation between serum copper levels and CVD risk, mortality, and disease progression [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

A systematic review and meta-analysis (16 observational studies, 41,322 participants; Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine, 2023) found that high serum copper levels were associated with increased risk of total stroke (pOR: 1.49, 95% CI 1.22–1.82), myocardial infarction (pOR: 1.31, 95% CI 1.17–1.46), and cardiovascular mortality (pOR: 1.60, 95% CI 1.39–1.86). No significant association was found for hemorrhagic stroke (pOR: 1.29, 95% CI 0.87–1.91). Monitoring of S-Cu levels, as an independent risk marker, could be an additional tool in the primary prevention of MACE [Serum copper levels and risk of MACE: Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine, 2023].

The St Andrews study (2025) found that high copper was associated with a higher risk of developing MACE, and high copper was associated with increased risks of various circulatory diseases [Abnormal plasma/serum magnesium, copper and zinc concentrations: Nutrients, 2025].

### 2.8 Copper Deficiency and Cardiovascular Disease

Copper deficiency causes mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS accumulation, myocardial I/R injury, ECG abnormalities, cardiac hypertrophy, impaired contractility, increased inflammation, anemia, and atherosclerosis. Dietary copper deficiency is widespread in Western populations [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

Low copper was specifically associated with heightened risk of venous and lymphatic disease [Abnormal plasma/serum magnesium, copper and zinc concentrations: Nutrients, 2025].

### 2.9 Copper and Cardiac Fibrosis / Cuproptosis

Copper ions mediate programmed cell death (cuproptosis) in cardiac fibrosis [Redox homeostasis in cardiac fibrosis: Redox Biology, 2024].

### 2.10 Therapeutic Approaches for Copper Modulation

- **Copper Chelators**: Triethylenetetramine (TETA), tetrathiomolybdate (TTM), disodium EDTA, and trientine — used to remove excess copper. Risks include redistribution of metals to the brain, loss of essential metals (zinc), and hepatotoxicity [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].
- **Small-Molecule Inhibitors**: DCAL50 inhibits copper chaperone proteins ATOX1 and CCS, blocking intracellular copper transport without affecting normal cells [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].
- **Copper Ion Carriers**: Elesclomol and disulfiram facilitate copper entry into cells, increasing ROS and triggering cell death. Used primarily in cancer research; cardiovascular applications require further study [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].
- **Natural Antidotes**: Herbal derivatives (e.g., turmeric/curcumin) show fewer side effects and higher stability than synthetic chelators [Copper Ions: The Invisible Killer of Cardiovascular Disease: Molecular Medicine Reports, 2024].

### 2.11 Copper in COPD

Copper is elevated in stable COPD (reflecting chronic inflammation), decreased during acute exacerbations [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

## 3. SELENIUM (Se)

### 3.1 General Background and Essentiality

Selenium (Se) is a vital trace element playing its biological functions through selenoproteins, which have been implicated in various physiological and pathological processes [Selenium concentration is associated with CVD: J Trace Elem Med Biol, 2022]. Selenium is a trace nutrient that promotes human health through its incorporation into selenoproteins in the form of the redox-active amino acid selenocysteine (Sec) [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021].

Unlike other essential trace elements that interact with proteins in the form of cofactors, selenium becomes co-translationally incorporated into the polypeptide chain as part of the 21st naturally occurring amino acid, selenocysteine (Sec), encoded by the UGA codon. There are 25 genes encoding for selenoproteins in humans [Selenium-Dependent Antioxidant Enzymes: Antioxidants, 2018].

The Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) of Se is 55 μg/day for men, 70 μg/day for women on lactation, though many European countries average below 40 μg/day [Selenium-Dependent Antioxidant Enzymes: Antioxidants, 2018]. The Frontiers in Physiology mini-review (2021) recommends 55 μg/day [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021].

### 3.2 Selenium as a Cofactor for Glutathione Peroxidases

Selenium is incorporated into 25 human selenoproteins as selenocysteine. Key selenoproteins involved in cardiovascular function include:

**Glutathione Peroxidases (GPx1, GPx3, GPx4):** These reduce hydrogen and lipid hydroperoxides.

- **GPx1** detoxifies intracellular H₂O₂ and protects against ischemia-reperfusion injury, homocysteine-induced endothelial dysfunction, Adriamycin/doxorubicin cardiotoxicity, and Keshan disease. GPx1 deficiency promotes endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis. GPx1 activity was a strong predictor of future cardiovascular (CV) events, with a hazard ratio of 0.29 (95% CI, 0.15–0.58; p < 0.001) for the lowest tertile compared to the highest tertile [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021].

- **GPx3** (plasma GPx) scavenges ROS in extracellular spaces, regulates NO bioavailability, and protects against stroke and thrombosis. GPx3 regulates platelet homeostasis and thrombosis [Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

- **GPx4** protects cellular lipids from oxidative damage. In mice, knockout of GPx4 results in embryonic lethality. Its inhibition can promote a form of cell death called ferroptosis that involves iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. GPx4 protects against ferroptosis and atherogenesis. GPx4 is upregulated in myocardial hypertrophy [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021; Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

### 3.3 Selenoproteins in Redox Regulation

**Thioredoxin Reductases (Txnrd1, Txnrd2):** Regulate redox state of thioredoxins. Txnrd2 is essential for cardiac development; its knockout causes fatal dilated cardiomyopathy in mice. Mutations in the human TXNRD2 gene that affect the flavin-adenine dinucleotide binding domain result in dilated cardiomyopathy [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021]. Txnrd1 is induced during myocardial hypertrophy [Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

**Selenoprotein P:** Transports Se to tissues; can impair angiogenesis by attenuating VEGF signaling [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021].

**Selenoprotein S and K:** ER-resident proteins. Selenoprotein S is protective against inflammation; Selenoprotein K may promote atherosclerosis by regulating oxidized LDL uptake in macrophages. SelK promotes foam cell formation and atherogenesis via CD36 expression in macrophages. SelS polymorphisms may affect cardiovascular disease risk [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021; Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

**MsrB1 (SelR):** Reduces methionine sulfoxide; influences macrophage function. MsrB1 was identified as one selenoprotein that was highly upregulated in hearts during cardiac stress; plays roles in reversing oxidative protein damage and regulating actin dynamics during cardiac remodeling [Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

**Deiodinases (DIO1-3):** Regulate thyroid hormone metabolism important for cardiac function [Selenoproteins and Cardiovascular Stress: Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 2015].

### 3.4 Selenium Deficiency and Cardiovascular Disease

Selenium deficiency is linked to Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy occurring in regions of China with low selenium availability [Selenium, a Micronutrient That Modulates Cardiovascular Health via Redox Enzymology: Nutrients, 2021; The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021]. Selenium deficiency leads to an increase in mRNA levels of caspase-3 and caspase-9 and a decrease in BCL-2 levels, which promotes cardiomyocyte death [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

A systematic review and meta-analysis (49 studies, 61 cohorts; J Trace Elem Med Biol, 2022) found that selenium levels were significantly lower in patients with heart failure (SMD = −0.98, 95% CI: −1.34 to −0.62), myocardial infarction (SMD = −3.46, 95% CI: −4.43 to −2.85), and coronary heart disease (SMD = −0.47, 95% CI: −0.64 to −0.28) compared to healthy controls. Se level was found to be a good diagnostic marker of MI (AUC = 0.7107, P = 0.0167, Sensitivity = 77.27%, Specificity = 72.73%) [Selenium concentration is associated with CVD: J Trace Elem Med Biol, 2022].

Higher selenium intake (>122 μg/day) was associated with lower COPD risk (OR 0.80) [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

A 50% increase in Se levels corresponded to a 24% reduction in coronary incident risk. Physiologically high Se levels were related to reduced CHD mortality (RR = 0.73) and incidence (RR = 0.83) [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

### 3.5 Selenium Excess and Toxicity

Excess selenium (>900 μg/day) can be toxic [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021]. NHANES data (2011-2016, n=6,683) showed serum Se ≥120 μg/L was associated with hypertension (OR=1.46), and levels >150 μg/L strengthened the association (OR=1.69). However, contradictory findings from NHANES 2003-2018 (n=32,928) indicated each quartile increase in dietary Se intake reduced hypertension likelihood by 11%. A U-shaped association was found between serum Se and mortality in hypertensive patients, with lowest mortality at 136 μg/L [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

### 3.6 Selenium Supplementation

Selenium supplementation reduced mechanical ventilation duration (9.4 vs. 17.8 days) and improved muscle strength in one study [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024]. However, randomized controlled trials showed Se supplementation did not reduce CHD mortality, though it increased GPx activity and decreased CRP levels [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

Antioxidant mixtures containing Se reduced cardiovascular mortality (RR = 0.77) [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

### 3.7 Selenium and Arrhythmias

In the PREVEND study (n=5,452 with Se measurements, 6.2-year follow-up), non-smokers with Se deficiency (<70 μg/L) had 68% higher risk of developing atrial fibrillation [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

### 3.8 Selenium in Heart Failure

A case-control study showed mean serum Se was 92.5 mg/dL in HF patients vs. 109.3 mg/dL in controls. A prospective cohort of 2,516 HF patients found >20% had Se <70 μg/L, associated with worse quality of life and prognosis [Selenium as a Modulator of Redox Reactions in CVD: Antioxidants, 2024].

### 3.9 Selenium in Rheumatoid Arthritis

RA patients exhibit significantly lower serum concentrations of Se compared to both control and MetD groups [Serum Levels of Trace Elements in RA: Biological Trace Element Research, 2024].

## 4. MAGNESIUM (Mg)

### 4.1 General Background and Essentiality

A 70 kg human contains 20-24 g of magnesium (60% in bones, 35% in soft tissues, only 1% in blood). Serum magnesium does not accurately reflect intracellular levels [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net]. The current RDA for magnesium is 420 mg daily for males and 320 mg daily for females above 31 years [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net]. The modern Western diet provides only 200-300 mg/day of magnesium, down from 410 mg at the beginning of the 20th century [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

It is estimated that 25% or more of the United States population experiences chronic, latent Mg²⁺ depletion [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024]. The United States estimated average requirement (EAR) for Mg²⁺ is 255 mg/day for women aged 19–30 years, 265 mg/day for women aged ≥31 years; for men aged 19–30 the EAR is 330 mg/day, increasing to 350 mg/day for men aged ≥31 years [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024].

### 4.2 Magnesium's Role in Vascular Tone and Blood Pressure Regulation

Magnesium is considered to be nature's physiologic calcium blocker [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net]. Mg²⁺ reduces vascular smooth muscle contraction by blocking L-type Ca²⁺ channels, supporting prostacyclin and nitric oxide (NO) release, and promoting vasodilation [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024]. Magnesium helps regulate vascular tone by relaxing blood vessels and reducing resistance in the arteries [How Magnesium Supports Cardiovascular Health: Dee Cee Laboratories, 2026].

Magnesium acts as a natural calcium channel blocker, increases nitric oxide, improves endothelial dysfunction, and induces direct and indirect vasodilation [The Role of Magnesium in Hypertension and CVD: J Clin Hypertension, 2011].

Five key mechanisms by which Mg²⁺ influences blood pressure [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024]:

1. **Vascular tone**: Mg²⁺ reduces vascular smooth muscle contraction by blocking L-type Ca²⁺ channels, supporting prostacyclin and nitric oxide (NO) release, and promoting vasodilation.
2. **Sympathetic tone**: Mg²⁺ attenuates sympathetic nervous system activity by modulating NMDA receptor activity in the brainstem and hypothalamus, and by blocking N-type Ca²⁺ channels at nerve endings, reducing catecholamine release.
3. **Renal K⁺ and Na⁺ handling**: Mg²⁺ depletion promotes urinary K⁺ wasting through loss of voltage-dependent blockade of ROMK channels, and influences aldosterone secretion.
4. **Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**: Mg²⁺ directly reduces aldosterone secretion from adrenal zona glomerulosa cells, and attenuates angiotensin II-stimulated aldosterone release.
5. **Pro-hypertensive inflammation**: Mg²⁺ depletion activates NLRP3 inflammasome and stimulates isolevuglandin (IsoLG) production in dendritic cells and macrophages, promoting inflammation that drives hypertension.

### 4.3 Magnesium Supplementation and Blood Pressure

Meta-analyses of clinical trials show that Mg²⁺ supplementation reduces systolic blood pressure by 2-5.78 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure by 1.78-2.5 mmHg, with greater effects in hypertensive individuals [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024].

Mg²⁺ supplementation of 365–450 mg/day for a mean of 3.6 months significantly reduced SBP by a mean of 4.18 mmHg and DBP by a mean of 2.27 mmHg [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024].

Magnesium intake of 500 mg/d to 1000 mg/d may reduce blood pressure (BP) as much as 5.6/2.8 mm Hg [The Role of Magnesium in Hypertension and CVD: J Clin Hypertension, 2011].

A 2016 RCT (Zhang et al.) found magnesium supplementation (~368 mg/day for 3 months) reduced systolic BP by 2.00 mm Hg and diastolic by 1.78 mm Hg in hypertensive adults. A 2025 meta-analysis (Argeros et al.) showed magnesium supplementation reduced systolic BP by -2.81 mm Hg and diastolic by -2.05 mm Hg overall, with stronger effects (up to -7.68 mm Hg systolic) in hypertensive individuals. A 2024 meta-analysis (Alharran et al.) found doses ≥400 mg/day associated with meaningful BP reductions [Magnesium and Blood Pressure Support: LifeSource Vitamins].

The combination of increased intake of magnesium and potassium coupled with reduced sodium intake is more effective in reducing BP than single mineral intake and is often as effective as one antihypertensive drug in treating hypertension [The Role of Magnesium in Hypertension and CVD: J Clin Hypertension, 2011].

It is recommended that 1000 mg of magnesium be combined with 4.7 g of potassium and <1.5 g of sodium per day through both diet and supplements to maximize BP reduction [The Role of Magnesium in Hypertension and CVD: J Clin Hypertension, 2011].

### 4.4 Magnesium's Role in Arrhythmias

Magnesium acts as a natural calcium channel blocker, regulating electrical impulses in the heart to prevent overexcitation of cardiac muscles, prevent irregular heartbeats, palpitations, and conditions like atrial fibrillation (AFib) [How Magnesium Supports Cardiovascular Health: Dee Cee Laboratories, 2026].

Magnesium therapy is indicated in life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias such as Torsades de Pointes and intractable ventricular tachycardia. Magnesium is recommended by the American Heart Association as the third drug of choice for pulseless VT/VF [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

### 4.5 Magnesium and Endothelial Function

Oral magnesium (730 mg/day for 6 months) significantly improved endothelial function, exercise duration, and reduced exercise-induced chest pain and arrhythmias [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

### 4.6 Magnesium and Platelet Function

A 3-month oral magnesium supplementation (800-1,200 mg/day) significantly reduced the median platelet-dependent thrombosis by 35% compared to placebo in stable CAD patients who were on aspirin therapy [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

### 4.7 Magnesium in Acute Myocardial Infarction

The LIMIT-2 trial (2,316 patients) showed 24% mortality reduction at 28 days and 20% reduction in ischemic heart disease mortality over 4.5 years. However, the larger ISIS-4 (58,000 patients) and MAGIC (6,213 patients) trials found no survival benefit from IV magnesium. Magnesium is not recommended for routine use in all AMI patients but may benefit high-risk groups (elderly, CHF patients, those ineligible for reperfusion therapy) [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

### 4.8 Magnesium Deficiency and Cardiovascular Risk

Abnormal magnesium levels were associated with a higher risk of developing MACE. Low magnesium was associated with increased risks of various circulatory diseases [Abnormal plasma/serum magnesium, copper and zinc concentrations: Nutrients, 2025].

Hypomagnesemia is common in hospitalized patients, especially elderly with CAD and/or chronic heart failure. It is associated with increased incidence of diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and mortality from CAD and all causes [Magnesium and cardiovascular system: Shechter, Cardiacos.net].

Higher circulating magnesium levels were associated with a 30% lower risk of cardiovascular disease events [Del Gobbo et al., 2013, cited in Magnesium and Blood Pressure Support: LifeSource Vitamins].

### 4.9 Magnesium and Cholesterol

Higher magnesium intake is associated with lower LDL ("bad") cholesterol and higher HDL ("good") cholesterol. It also helps prevent oxidative damage to LDL cholesterol that contributes to arterial plaque buildup [How Magnesium Supports Cardiovascular Health: Dee Cee Laboratories, 2026].

### 4.10 Magnesium in COPD

Intravenous magnesium sulfate during exacerbations improved lung function (FEV1, FVC, PEFR) and bronchodilation when combined with beta-agonists, though standalone effectiveness varied [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

### 4.11 Clinical Recommendations for Magnesium

Clinicians should have a high index of suspicion for Mg²⁺-depletion in hypertensive patients, given that: (1) dietary Mg²⁺ deficiency is common, (2) hypertension is associated with Mg²⁺ depletion, even in untreated patients, (3) common comorbidities (such as diabetes mellitus) are also associated with Mg²⁺ depletion, and (4) commonly prescribed medications promote Mg²⁺ deficiency, including thiazide-type and loop diuretics, and proton pump inhibitors [Magnesium in hypertension: Frontiers in Physiology, 2024].

## 5. IRON (Fe)

### 5.1 General Background and Essentiality

Iron is essential for oxygen transport via hemoglobin and myoglobin. The recommended daily intake is 18 mg/day for women and 10 mg/day for men [Trace Elements - Diet and Health: NCBI Bookshelf, 1989]. Iron deficiency is the most prevalent malnutrition-related condition and affects up to 75% of patients with heart failure [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].

### 5.2 Iron's Role in Oxidative Stress

Iron overload correlates with increased oxidative stress, cardiovascular risks, and potential cancer progression [The emerging role of iron, zinc, copper, magnesium and selenium: Biogenic Amines, 2005]. Free Fe²⁺ reacts with hydrogen peroxide via the Fenton reaction to generate lipid peroxides, driving oxidative damage [An emerging double-edged sword role of ferroptosis in CVD: IJMM, 2024].

### 5.3 Iron Metabolism in the Heart

Iron uptake in cardiomyocytes depends on TFR1-mediated endocytosis of transferrin-bound iron. Iron export is mediated by ferroportin (the only known iron exporter). The hepcidin-ferroportin axis is crucial for cardiac iron homeostasis. Key iron regulatory proteins include IRP1, IRP2, ferritin, NCOA4 (ferritinophagy), and tristetraprolin. Mice lacking Tfr1 in the heart have severe cardiomyopathy with cardiac iron deficiency and die in the second week of life [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].

### 5.4 Iron Overload-Associated Cardiac Disorders

- **Hereditary haemochromatosis**: Common inherited disorder causing iron overload and heart failure [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].
- **Friedreich ataxia**: Caused by FXN gene mutations, leading to mitochondrial iron accumulation and cardiomyopathy [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].
- **Thalassaemia**: Transfusion-induced iron overload causing cardiomyopathy [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].
- **Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity**: Doxorubicin causes mitochondrial iron accumulation; >25% of patients receiving 550 mg/m² develop congestive heart failure [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].
- **Dietary iron overload**: High haem iron intake correlated with increased cardiovascular risk [The molecular and metabolic landscape of iron and ferroptosis in CVD: Nature Reviews Cardiology, 2023].

### 5.5 Ferroptosis: Iron-Dependent Cell Death

Ferroptosis is a recently identified form of regulated cell death, distinct from apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and autophagy-dependent cell death. It is characterized by iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation [Ferroptosis: a cell death connecting oxidative stress, inflammation and CVD: Cell Death Discovery, 2021].

Three essential features of ferroptosis: dysfunction of lipid peroxide clearance, presence of redox-active iron, and oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-containing phospholipids [Ferroptosis: a cell death connecting oxidative stress, inflammation and CVD: Cell Death Discovery, 2021].

The core regulatory pathway involves the cystine/glutamate antiporter (system Xc⁻), glutathione (GSH), and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4). Depletion of GSH or inactivation of GPX4 leads to accumulation of lipid peroxides and ferroptosis. Iron accumulation drives ferroptosis through Fenton chemistry and lipoxygenase-mediated lipid peroxidation. A second ferroptosis-suppression pathway involving FSP1 (ferroptosis suppressor protein 1) and CoQ10 has also been identified [Ferroptosis: a cell death connecting oxidative stress, inflammation and CVD: Cell Death Discovery, 2021].

The enzyme GPX4 tightly mediates the ferroptosis surveillance mechanism. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of lipid peroxides to their respective alcohols, preventing their accumulation and playing a protective role in cells. Glutathione is an essential cofactor for GPX4 functioning [Ferroptosis in CVD and Cardiomyopathies: Biomedicines, 2024].

### 5.6 Ferroptosis in Cardiovascular Diseases

**Atherosclerosis:** Ferroptosis in endothelial cells and macrophages contributes to endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and foam cell formation. Inhibition of ferroptosis (e.g., by ferrostatin-1) alleviates atherosclerosis in mouse models. GPX4 overexpression and iron chelation both show protective effects. Iron overload catalyzes lipid ROS, oxidizes LDL, promotes foam cell formation, and endothelial dysfunction [Ferroptosis: a cell death connecting oxidative stress, inflammation and CVD: Cell Death Discovery, 2021; An emerging double-edged sword role of ferroptosis in CVD: IJMM, 2024].

**Myocardial Infarction and Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury (I/RI):** Ferroptosis occurs mainly during reperfusion rather than ischemia. GPX4 levels decrease during MI. mTOR, USP22/SIRT1/p53/SLC7A11, and USP7 pathways regulate ferroptosis. Liproxstatin-1 and iron chelators reduce injury. Ferroptosis is most prominent during reperfusion phase due to oxidative burst. Involves ER stress via PERK/eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP pathway [The Emerging Role of Ferroptosis in CVD: Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2022; An emerging double-edged sword role of ferroptosis in CVD: IJMM, 2024].

**Heart Failure:** Erastin/isoprenaline-induced ferroptosis in H9C2 cells; doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy involves Nrf2/Hmox1-mediated iron overload. Puerarin and Acot1 show protective effects [The Emerging Role of Ferroptosis in CVD: Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2022].

**Cardiomyopathy:** Multiple forms including chemotherapy-induced (DOX via NRF2/HMOX1 pathway), radiation-induced (ACSL4 upregulation), septic, COVID-19-related (GPX4 reduction, ORF3a degrading NRF2), diabetic, hypertensive, sickle cell disease, hypertrophic, dilated, post-transplant, and iron overload cardiomyopathy [An emerging double-edged sword role of ferroptosis in CVD: IJMM, 2024].

Cardiac myocytes rely almost exclusively on aerobic respiration to meet their energy needs. Oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria is the primary mode of ATP generation in these cells, accounting for approximately 95% of the heart's ATP production [Ferroptosis in CVD and Cardiomyopathies: Biomedicines, 2024].

### 5.7 Iron Metabolism and Cardiac Fibrosis

Iron ions metabolism plays a key role in cardiac fibrosis through ROS triggered by iron deposition in cardiomyocytes [Redox homeostasis in cardiac fibrosis: Redox Biology, 2024].

### 5.8 Iron in COPD

Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose improved exercise capacity (6MWD increased by 34.7m), quality of life (CAT scores), and reduced oxidative stress markers in non-anemic iron-deficient COPD patients [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

## 6. CALCIUM (Ca)

### 6.1 General Background

Required intake of calcium is 1,200-1,500 mg/day [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021].

### 6.2 Calcium's Role in Vascular Calcification

Vascular calcification (VC) is associated with aging, cardiovascular and renal diseases and results in poor morbidity and increased mortality. VC is a complex, active and cell-mediated process involving the transdifferentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) to a bone-like phenotype, systemic inflammation, decreased anti-calcific events (loss of calcification inhibitors), loss in SMC lineage markers and enhanced pro-calcific microRNAs (miRs), an increased intracellular calcium level, apoptosis, aberrant DNA damage response (DDR) and senescence of vascular SMCs [Vascular Calcification Mechanisms: Biomedicines, 2021].

High serum phosphate (Pi) level is related to pathologies which affect the behavior of vascular cells, including platelets, endothelial cells (ECs) and smooth muscle cells (SMCs), and plays a central role in promoting VC. Pi-mediated signaling pathways include: oxidative stress (ROS production, NF-κB activation via RelA/p65), oxidative DNA damage, cellular senescence (via ILK overexpression, p53/p21/p16 upregulation, SA-β-gal activity), and increased intracellular calcium levels (via SOCE, STIM1/ORAI1 upregulation) [Vascular Calcification Mechanisms: Biomedicines, 2021].

Even though VC was originally thought to be a passive process of ectopic deposition of calcium/phosphate minerals within the vascular wall, it is now well-documented that VC is an active cell-mediated process involving transdifferentiation of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) into bone-like phenotypes [Vascular Calcification Mechanisms: Biomedicines, 2021].

Ectopic calcification (mineralization outside the skeleton) commonly occurs in diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and atherosclerotic heart disease, leading to increased mortality and morbidity. No therapies currently exist for retarding or attenuating ectopic calcification in heart valves or blood vessels. Artery wall calcification was previously considered a passive degenerative process; work now indicates that artery wall cells actively form calcium deposits in much the same way that skeletal bone cells form mineral [UCLA Medical School - Vascular Calcification].

### 6.3 VSMC Osteogenic Differentiation

Approximately 98% of osteochondrogenic cells expressing Runx2 in atherosclerotic plaques were derived from VSMCs. VSMC-derived cells constitute a substantial proportion (30%–70%) of all plaque cells. VSMC phenotypic switching is regulated by transcription factors including SRF, MYOCD, KLF4, OCT4, and TCF21. The BMP signaling pathway (both canonical Smad-dependent and non-canonical p38 MAPK pathways) plays a central role in osteochondrogenic differentiation [Roles of VSMCs in Atherosclerotic Calcification: J Lipid Atherosclerosis, 2023].

Thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP) was identified as a critical regulator of the osteochondrogenic switch of VSMCs. TXNIP deficiency in hyperlipidemic mice enhances the phenotypic transition of modulated VSMCs toward the osteochondrogenic population by upregulating canonical and non-canonical BMP signaling, leading to plaque calcification [Roles of VSMCs in Atherosclerotic Calcification: J Lipid Atherosclerosis, 2023].

### 6.4 Calcium's Role in VSMC Elasticity and Adhesion

Intracellular Ca²⁺ ([Ca²⁺]i) directly manipulates the expressions of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and α5β1 integrin, and the α5β1 integrin regulates [Ca²⁺]i level in accordance with physiological requirement. This operates parallel to the Ca²⁺-CaM-MLCK pathway to influence VSMC stiffness and adhesion via ECM-integrin-cytoskeletal axis without any cascade cycles by phosphorylation and dephosphorylation. Increasing [Ca²⁺]i (via ionomycin or angiotensin II) promotes α-SMA production, F-actin assembly, and α5β1 integrin expression, leading to increased VSMC stiffness and adhesion to fibronectin matrix. Conversely, decreasing [Ca²⁺]i (via BAPTA-AM) reduces these effects [Calcium in VSMC Elasticity and Adhesion: Frontiers in Physiology, 2019].

The α5β1 integrin serves as the primary fibronectin receptor, providing mechanical linkage between the ECM and cytoskeleton. The increase in arterial stiffness is attributable to the dynamic changes of VSMC stiffness and adhesion process, opening up a new treatment for VSMC stiffness treatment of arteriosclerosis [Calcium in VSMC Elasticity and Adhesion: Frontiers in Physiology, 2019].

### 6.5 Calcium and Cardiac Fibrosis

Dysregulation of calcium ion homeostasis contributes to cardiac fibrosis via multiple factors causing excess calcium influx [Redox homeostasis in cardiac fibrosis: Redox Biology, 2024].

### 6.6 Calcium and Calcification Types

Microcalcifications and spotty calcifications are associated with plaque instability, while macrocalcifications may stabilize plaques. Calcified nodules (up to 5% of thrombosis cases) are associated with worse clinical outcomes and high recurrence rates after stenting [Roles of VSMCs in Atherosclerotic Calcification: J Lipid Atherosclerosis, 2023]. The coronary artery calcium (CAC) score can be used as a sensitive and specific predictor of clinically significant coronary artery disease and identify patients at risk for adverse cardiac events [Roles of VSMCs in Atherosclerotic Calcification: J Lipid Atherosclerosis, 2023].

### 6.7 Calcium Supplementation and Cardiovascular Risk

Calcium supplements cause a surge in the ionized and total serum calcium levels in a short interval of time after ingestion and this increases the levels of insoluble calciprotein particles which are calcification activators in the serum that may lead to vascular calcification and myocardial infarction. Dietary calcium appears protective, but calcium supplements may increase risks of vascular calcification, coronary artery disease, and myocardial infarction. The authors recommend relying on dietary sources over supplements [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021].

## 7. LESS COMMONLY DISCUSSED METAL IONS

### 7.1 Chromium (Cr)

Trivalent Cr is biologically active; hexavalent Cr is toxic. Hexavalent Cr is a respiratory carcinogen causing a broad spectrum of DNA breaks, thus having both genotoxic and mutagenic effects. Cr(VI) is classified as a Group I carcinogen (IARC). Deficiency of Cr is associated with diabetes-like symptoms; Cr supplementation may improve glucose tolerance. The recommended daily intake is 35 μg/day in adults. Cr is transported bound to transferrin and albumin; competes with iron for transferrin binding. Reference interval for serum/plasma: <10 nmol/L (<0.5 μg/L) [Chapter 10: Trace Elements, Clinical Laboratory Diagnostics].

A systematic review from Johns Hopkins (2016) identified only 5 articles on chromium and cardiovascular disease, concluding the current evidence is insufficient to inform on the cardiovascular role of these metals because of the small number of studies [Environmental Metals and CVD in Adults: Current Environmental Health Reports, 2016].

In a mixture effects study (Scientific Reports, 2024), chromium, nickel, and zinc levels were associated with CVD. For T2D, the mixture effect was significantly associated with T2D (OR 11.96, 95% CI 5.65–18.26), with chromium having a weight of 0.17 in the model [Mixture effects of trace element levels on CVD and T2D: Scientific Reports, 2024].

### 7.2 Manganese (Mn)

Manganese is essential for Mn-SOD (SOD2, the mitochondrial antioxidant defense enzyme). Three types of mammalian SOD exist: SOD1 (cytoplasmic Cu/Zn), SOD2 (mitochondrial matrix Mn), and SOD3 (extracellular Cu/Zn) [Cu/Zn Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1): Chemistry LibreTexts].

In the AHA Scientific Sessions 2025 study, manganese dominated the mixture component for CHD risk (76.9%) [Cadmium Is a Major Contributor to Toxic Metal-Associated Risk for CVD: AHA 2025].

Evidence on manganese levels in COPD patients is mixed. Synergistic effects with other antioxidants are noted [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

The exogenous supplementation of metal ions such as Mn²⁺ exhibits antioxidant properties by reducing ROS, activating antioxidant pathways (e.g., Keap1-Nrf2), and upregulating antioxidant enzymes [Exogeneous metal ions as therapeutic agents in CVD: Regenerative Biomaterials, 2023].

### 7.3 Vanadium (V)

Vanadium is considered a "probably essential" trace element. The systematic review from Johns Hopkins (2016) identified 0 articles on vanadium and cardiovascular disease, concluding the current evidence is not sufficient to inform on the cardiovascular role of vanadium due to the small number of studies [Environmental Metals and CVD in Adults: Current Environmental Health Reports, 2016].

### 7.4 Cadmium (Cd)

Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal that has been associated with many diseases. Cd production increased during the 20th century as a result of the production of nickel-cadmium batteries, metal coatings and plastic stabilizers. Cd is an environmental contaminant classified eighth on the Top 20 Hazardous Substances Priority List because of its high toxicity and sluggish metabolism [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021].

**Exposure Sources:** Tobacco smoke is considered to be the most significant source of cadmium exposure, and smokers have approximately twice the cadmium body burden of nonsmokers. Exposure occurs through contaminated food (leafy vegetables, grains), drinking water, and polluted air. Cd has a biological half-life of 10-30 years and accumulates mainly in kidneys, liver, and bones [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021; Cadmium Exposure: Mechanisms and Pathways: Toxics, 2024].

**Mechanisms of Toxicity:** Cd is transported in blood bound to metallothionein. It causes damage by inducing lipid peroxidation, disturbing antioxidant systems, disrupting endothelial integrity, promoting inflammation (via IL-6, IL-8, IL-1β, TNF-α), and stimulating smooth muscle cell proliferation, thereby accelerating atherosclerosis [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021].

Cd disrupts cellular functions through four key toxic mechanisms: (1) oxidative stress (disrupting electron transport chain, activating NADPH oxidase, impairing antioxidant enzymes), (2) signal transduction disruption (interfering with MAPK, NF-κB, and p53 pathways, and disrupting Ca²⁺ signaling by mimicking calcium), (3) epigenetic alterations (altering DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA expression), and (4) interference with calcium, zinc, and iron homeostasis [Cadmium Exposure: Mechanisms and Pathways: Toxics, 2024].

Messner et al. identified Cd as a novel and independent risk factor for the development of atherosclerosis. The pro-atherosclerotic effect of Cd was shown to be due to the inhibition of cell proliferation as well as the induction of DNA damage-induced cell death [The Role of Trace Elements in CVD: Toxics, 2023].

**Epidemiological Evidence:** The pooled relative risks (95% CI) for CVD, coronary heart disease, stroke, and peripheral arterial disease due to cadmium exposure were 1.36 (95% CI: 1.11-1.66), 1.30 (95% CI: 1.12-1.52), 1.18 (95% CI: 0.86-1.59), and 1.49 (95% CI: 1.15-1.92), respectively [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021].

In the mixture effects study (Scientific Reports, 2024), Cd had the highest weight among the metals in the CVD model (weighted at 0.78), followed by Hg weighted at 0.197. The weight quartile sum (WQS) index was significantly associated with both CVD (OR 4.17, 95% CI 2.16–7.69) [Mixture effects of trace element levels on CVD and T2D: Scientific Reports, 2024].

At the AHA Scientific Sessions 2025, researchers found that among five toxic metals, cadmium exposure is the most significant driver of elevated CVD risk. In single-metal models, increased cadmium levels were associated with higher risk for MI (OR 1.43), angina (OR 1.26), and stroke (OR 1.16). In mixture models, cadmium contributed the most to stroke risk (67.6%) and CHF risk (63.5%), while manganese dominated CHD risk (76.9%) [Cadmium Is a Major Contributor to Toxic Metal-Associated Risk for CVD: AHA 2025].

**Cadmium as a Predictive Biomarker:** Day 1 urinary cadmium levels (D1UCd) have shown strong predictive ability for mortality in patients with acute heart failure and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Each 1-μg increase in D1UCd was associated with a 1.5-fold increased risk of 30-day mortality in AMI patients. D1UCd may outperform established scoring systems like SOFA and APACHE II [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021].

**Chelation Therapy:** The Trial to Assess Chelation Therapy (TACT) showed that EDTA chelation therapy modestly reduced adverse cardiovascular outcomes in stable patients with a history of AMI [Cadmium and cardiovascular disease: Rev Port Cardiol, 2021].

## 8. MIXTURE EFFECTS AND INTERACTIONS

### 8.1 Multi-Trace Element Supplementation

A randomized controlled trial of 96 critically ill participants found that intravenous supplementation of multi-trace elements (zinc, copper, selenium, chromium, and manganese) significantly improved outcomes: 28-day mortality was 18 deaths in the interventional group vs 32 in the control group; 90-day mortality was 20 vs 35; mean ICU stay was lower for the interventional group (10.60±3.42 days) vs controls (16.83±3.00 days) (p<0.0001) [Effects of parenterally administered trace elements: European Journal of Cardiovascular Medicine, 2023].

### 8.2 Mixture Effects from the RaNCD Cohort

A study using G-computation analysis (450 participants; Scientific Reports, 2024) found that the mixture effect of nine trace elements (As, Cd, Hg, Pb, Ni, Cr, Cu, Fe, Zn) was significantly associated with CVD (OR 4.17, 95% CI 2.16–7.69) and T2D (OR 11.96, 95% CI 5.65–18.26). Cd had the highest weight in the CVD model (0.78), followed by Hg (0.197). For T2D, the most weighted elements were Pb (0.32), Ni (0.19), Cr (0.17), and Cd (0.14) [Mixture effects of trace element levels on CVD and T2D: Scientific Reports, 2024].

### 8.3 Hair Mineral Analysis

Hair mineral analysis (HMA) has emerged as a promising non-invasive method for assessing long-term exposure to trace elements and metals. Patients with CVD consistently exhibit elevated levels of toxic elements (As, Hg, Pb, Cd, Ni, Al) and reduced concentrations of protective essential micronutrients (Mg, Mn, Zn, Cu, Fe, Cr, Li) in hair samples. ICP-MS with collision/reaction cell technology and microwave digestion are gold-standard analytical approaches. The greatest challenge remains the lack of widespread standardization of procedures and the limited availability of reference values adapted to biological and environmental variability [Essential and Toxic Elements in CVD: IJMS, 2025].

### 8.4 General Principles from Supplementation Trials

The Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular Journal review (2019) concluded that the evidence to date fails to support the use of exogenous supplements of vitamins and minerals for the prevention or treatment of cardiovascular disease in individuals without dietary deficiencies. The USPSTF currently does not recommend use of multivitamins for prevention of cardiovascular diseases. Beta-carotene should not be used for cardiovascular disease or cancer prevention; this is especially true for smokers due to an increased incidence of lung cancer. Folic acid has a possible role in stroke prevention, especially in populations with low baseline folate levels or in areas that lack folic acid fortification in foods. Dietary vitamin and mineral supplements are not benign; major and minor adverse effects have been reported in the RCTs discussed [Supplemental Vitamins and Minerals for CVD Prevention: Methodist DeBakey Cardiovascular J, 2019].

### 8.5 Exogenous Metal Ions as Therapeutic Agents

A review in Regenerative Biomaterials (2023) discusses the therapeutic potential of exogenous metal ions in CVD treatment covering three main therapeutic mechanisms: (1) Protecting cells from oxidative stress—metal ions such as Mg²⁺, Sr²⁺, Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺, and Cu²⁺ exhibit antioxidant properties by reducing ROS, activating antioxidant pathways (e.g., Keap1-Nrf2), and upregulating antioxidant enzymes. (2) Inducing angiogenesis—Cu²⁺, Mg²⁺, Co²⁺, Sr²⁺, and Ag⁺ promote blood vessel formation through upregulation of VEGF, HIF-1α, eNOS, and other growth factors, critical for ischemic heart disease recovery. (3) Adjusting ion channel functions—Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ regulate calcium, potassium, and other ion channels affecting cardiac conduction, vascular tension, and myocardial contractility. The article emphasizes that controllable local delivery is essential to maximize therapeutic benefits while minimizing toxicity associated with excessive metal ion supplementation [Exogeneous metal ions as therapeutic agents in CVD: Regenerative Biomaterials, 2023].

## 9. ENVIRONMENTAL HEAVY METALS AND CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE

An accumulating body of evidence from both experimental and observational studies implicates exposure to heavy metals, in a dose-response manner, in the increased risk of CVD. The limitations of most existing studies include insufficient statistical power, lack of comprehensive assessment of exposure, and cross-sectional design [Environmental heavy metals and CVD: Chronic Diseases and Translational Medicine, 2020].

Heavy metals disrupt cellular events including growth, proliferation, differentiation, damage-repairing processes, and apoptosis. Comparison of the mechanisms of action reveals similar pathways for these metals to induce toxicity including ROS generation, weakening of the antioxidant defense, enzyme inactivation, and oxidative stress. Some toxic metals including chromium, cadmium, and arsenic cause genomic instability and DNA repair defects, contributing to their carcinogenicity [Toxic Mechanisms of Five Heavy Metals: Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2021].

## 10. TRACE ELEMENTS IN SPECIFIC DISEASE CONTEXTS

### 10.1 Rheumatoid Arthritis and CVD Risk

Patients with RA experience an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), estimated to be 50% greater than that of the general population, with a mortality rate 1.5 times greater. RA patients exhibit significantly lower serum concentrations of Se than patients in both the control and MetD groups. Sr and Zn concentrations were independently associated with an increased Augmentation Index (AIx) in RA patients, showing that increased concentrations of both Sr and Zn were associated with an increased AIx (β = 2.40, P = 0.036 and β = 0.059, P = 0.005, respectively). Strontium levels in male RA patients were inversely associated with carotid intima-media thickness (cIMT) (β = -80.95, P = 0.028), suggesting a protective effect. This study represents the first report of the associations of Sr and Zn with the AIx and cIMT in RA patients [Serum Levels of Trace Elements in RA: Biological Trace Element Research, 2024].

### 10.2 COPD and Trace Elements

Trace elements, e.g., zinc, magnesium, and selenium, play key roles in COPD by regulating oxidative stress, inflammation, and immune responses. Supplementation with these elements can reduce inflammation, improve lung function, and enhance muscle strength in COPD patients. The minerals zinc, copper, iron, magnesium, manganese, selenium, and calcium may contribute to beneficial effects as part of the standard therapeutic management of COPD [The Role of Trace Elements in COPD: Nutrients, 2024].

## 11. DIETARY RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS

It is advisable to restrict the use of supplements, owing to the potent risks they may cause. Based on the large observational studies and available data, there definitely is an important role of the micronutrients calcium, zinc, vitamin D, and selenium on cardiovascular health. However, high circulating levels of these micronutrients have a detrimental effect on heart health as evidenced in some studies. It is, therefore, advisable to depend on dietary sources to meet the daily requirement of micronutrients [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021].

Both deficiency and excess of these micronutrients can harm cardiovascular health. Supplements cause rapid, sustained increases in serum levels that may be detrimental. The authors advise obtaining micronutrients from dietary sources rather than supplements until more clinical research is conducted [The Impact of Micronutrients: Frontiers in Physiology, 2021].
